lyrics:
There is a manual
I want to be clear about that
There is one
I found it
Page one
Big letters
Nothing else on the page
Figure out what works for you

Page two is blank
So is three
So is four
So is every page after that
I checked the back
Under the jacket
Held it to the window
Somebody printed
four hundred blank pages
and bound them properly
Somebody paid for that

Reed the manual
I red the manual
Cover to cover
Twice
Out loud
Figure out
what works for you

Went forward at an altar call
and meant every word
Six good weeks
Then
pray on it, son
See what the Lord puts on your heart
Two years with a therapist—
and she was good
I want that on the REK-ord—
and at the end she asked
what I thought would work for me
Ten days silent
Did it properly
Didn't cheat once
Last day
go find your own practice

Reed the manual
I red the manual
Cover to cover
Twice
Out loud
Figure out
what works for you

So I went further back
Greek
Encyclopedia
A line a night
Over the door
before the door was old

NOH-thee say-OW-tahn
Know Yourself
Two and a half thousand years
and the front of the building
still says the same thing
The page behind it
is still blank

Somebody did this
Somebody worked it out
and stopped
That's all I want
One person who's finished
I have sat in every room
and every room turns round at the end
and hands it back
One sentence
Four hundred empty pages
Where's the fucking manual
Nobody filled it in
Nobody ever filled it in

Everywhere they said to go
I went
Page two
Pen

what works for you

NOH-thee say-OW-tahn.

what works for you.
style: Progressive rock, Canterbury scene: angular ticking guitar-and-bass unison in odd meter, clipped organ jabs and alto saxophone interjections; resonant dry male baritone with understated wry delivery; syncopated phrasing over tight nervous grooves; warm live-ensemble production with gated room ambience, building breakdowns into a quiet hollowed-out outro, ‑autotune, ‑polished production

  Approved critic summary: Rose opens with a mumbled false start on 'I'm Old Now,' and that small, deliberate stumble tells you exactly what kind of record this is: nothing performed, nothing smoothed over, just a man taking honest stock.

  Approved critic summary: "A Distant Memory" opens with a counted-off "one, two, three, four" that sets a brisk 4/4 in C major, and from there Rose lets a female vocal float above a clean, roomy groove that leans more toward jazzy indie-pop than any straight ballad.
- 2026-06-25 — You Know Enough (single)
  Approved critic summary: There's a bat by the bed in this one, his father's before him, and nobody in the family has ever swung it.
- 2026-07-08 — You Don't Say (single)
  Approved critic summary: Nearly seven minutes, and Rose earns every one of them here by treating silence itself as the subject.
- 2026-07-18 — Outlandia (album)
  Approved critic summary: For a songwriter introduced as a diarist, a philosopher of the ordinary who finds a lifetime in a reflection on a phone screen, "Outlandia" is a startling pivot: a two-hour rock opera, twenty-four scenes long, about how a country is bought, broken, and inventoried.
- 2026-08-20 — Them Bones (single)
  Approved critic summary: After the two-hour sprawl of "Outlandia," Rose narrows the lens back down to something you can hold in one hand, and "Them Bones" benefits from the compression.
- 2026-08-30 — Unreasonably Quiet (single)
  Approved critic summary: Rose builds this one on a 3/4 pulse at a brisk clip, which is the first surprise: a waltz that never asks you to sway, driven instead by a Hammond groove and gritty guitar working against the meter rather than settling into it.
- 2026-09-12 — Wazoo In Effigy (album)
  Approved critic summary: Michael Anthony Rose’s *Wazoo in Effigy* is inspired by Frank Zappa, which is not quite the same thing as being a Zappa tribute.
- 2026-09-18 — The Grounding Post (single)
  Approved critic summary: Rose has spent 2026 moving between sprawling ambition and compressed intimacy, and 'The Grounding Post' lands firmly in the second register, closer in spirit to the quiet honesty of 'I'm Still Here' than to the operatic scale of 'Outlandia.' The track runs 3:29 in F# major, built on dry, close-miked fingerpicking and a baritone vocal that has the stillness of someone writing in the early morning before anyone else is awake.

impression.text: This track bursts with a theatrical, jazz-rock atmosphere, driven by an urgent and deeply expressive male vocal performance. The energy is relentlessly high and narrative-driven, propelling the listener through a labyrinth of intricate rhythms and anthemic crests. The production is remarkably dense yet pristine, allowing the razor-sharp drum fills, complex synth runs, and aggressive basslines to interlock perfectly without crowding the soaring lead vocal. A defining characteristic of the arrangement is its blistering progressive-fusion instrumental breaks, culminating in an explosive climax that fully unleashes the song's built-up tension.

review.review_text: The joke is right there in the title, and Rose earns it: a manual with page one printed in big letters, "Figure out what works for you," and "four hundred blank pages" bound properly behind it. He runs the deadpan through every room that ever handed him back an empty page, altar call, therapist, ten days silent, then the Greek over the temple door, "Know Yourself," and "the page behind it is still blank." At 152 in G# minor the Canterbury machinery does exactly what this kind of song needs, angular guitar-and-bass unison and clipped organ jabs keeping the nervous 4/4 taut while the baritone stays flat and methodical until the breakdown cracks it open on "Where's the fucking manual." The outro that hollows out to "Page two. Pen." and nothing else. This holds the room.
